segments.text: Hi guys, in this hands-on, we're going  to go into the management console,
and we're going to look at how we can use  AWS Systems Manager to manage EC2 instances.
The first thing I want to do is create an IAM  role. Now the reason for that is there's two
things we need to be able to manage our instances  with Systems Manager. The first one is the agent,
and that's going to be already installed on the  AMI we use, and then there's a role. The role
will give the EC2 instance the permissions  it needs to talk to Systems Manager.
So, I'm going to create a role. It's going  to be for EC2, so that EC2 can actually call
Systems Manager. And for policy, if we just  search for SSM, we'll find this policy here,
and SSM comes from an older name for Systems  Manager. So we can select this policy, and if you
want to look at the policy, you'll see that it has  lots of permissions to Systems Manager. So with
the policy selected, I'm going to click on Next,  click on Review, and I'm actually going to call it
the same name as the policy. So that's Amazon  EC2 role for SSM, and let's create the role.
So we've got our role created. Now we need to go  to EC2 and launch an instance. In EC2, I'm going
to launch an instance. Now, the Amazon Linux 2  AMI already comes with the SSM agent, as well as
the Windows option here as well. So we can choose  either one of these. Let's choose the Windows
option to make things a little bit different. So,  I'm going to choose the Windows Server 2019 base.
Once selected, I'm going to use t2.micro, and  then I need to make sure that I use my role.
So that's the Amazon EC2 role for SSM.  With that selected, let's click on Next,
come through to Security Group, choose our web  access, and then we'll launch our instance.
So the instance is launching. It has the  permissions it needs for Systems Manager,
and it has the agent pre-installed on it, so  that should be everything we need. We can now go
to Systems Manager, and within a few minutes, we  should start seeing some information populated.
Now, in Systems Manager, you'll probably get put  on the Quick Setup page when you first arrive,
and all you have to do there is just click on  Create, and it will automatically have this
host management option. You click on Next and  essentially just finish—you don't have to change
any settings—and then you'll have this  host management configuration type here.
So now it will take a few minutes for our  instance to actually report information,
but when it does, we should be able to  find some information about its inventory
under the Node Management Inventory tab here.
After a few minutes, I can see that a small amount  of information has been populated. We now know
that we have the Windows operating system version  here, and some more information may come soon.
Now what I want to do is go down to  Documents, and under Documents here,
we have all these documents we can  use with Run Command and Automation.
Now, I'm just going to search for the word  "stop," and it's filtered the list of results,
and I've got this option here to stop an  EC2 instance. In the document configuration,
we can see that it applies to Windows, as  well as Linux and macOS, so that's good.
And what I want to do is click Execute Automation.  There's various options here; I'm going to leave
it on Simple Execution, and then for Instance  ID, I'm going to check this little box here,
and we can see our instance. Now often you can  search by tags as well, which is a good way
to actually use automation. So, with our  instance selected, I'm going to click on Execute,
and hopefully, that should stop our EC2 instance  because we now have it under management control.
It has the agent, and so all we need to do is  actually run this command from Systems Manager.
And we can see that this is being executed; it's  in progress. And back on EC2 here, I've just
refreshed my page, and it's this bottom instance  here. We can see it's in the stopping state now,
and once the instance is fully  stopped, we get a success message.
So now if we want to start it up  again, we can go back to Documents,
search for "start," and "Start EC2 Instances" is  the one we want. So now we'll just execute this
automation again, choosing the instance we have,  and what we want to do here is show all instances
because it's in a stopped state. And so this is  the instance, the one I just stopped. We can see
it has the instance profile attached to it. So  then let's click on Execute. It's been initiated,
and back in EC2, if I click on Refresh, I've now  got a pending, so that's starting back up again.
So that's a very simple demonstration of how  to use Systems Manager. Now, as you can see,
there's lots more documents in there. You can do  things like scan for patches and install patches
and various other activities as well. And that's  it for this hands-on lesson. So all I need to do
to clean up is just terminate my EC2 instance,
and there's nothing else that we created  that's going to cost us any money.
